_comment: The first History Writer series: Seattle, five stories each. Ids for the first two match theme slugs already live on mchatai.com/seattle-landmarks, whose links have been shared; never rename them without keeping the old slug as an alias. Scout hints name KINDS of lives and collections to search, never specific people: who belongs in a series is decided by a dossier and an adversarial identity check, not by this file.

series.title: Women Who Built Seattle
series.membership: Women whose own work — founding, organising, building, teaching, healing, publishing, running a business or an institution — shaped the city.
sensitivity: A woman is the subject, not a husband's or father's footnote; name her by her own name, and give married and birth names when the record does.
Do not infer gender identity from a name; use the identity the person's own record shows.

series.title: Black Seattle
series.membership: Black Seattleites, established by self-identification or a reliable biography.
scoutHints: the first holders of public offices
business owners in Pioneer Square and the Central District
musicians of the Jackson Street era
sensitivity: Identity by evidence only — never inferred from a surname, a photograph or a neighbourhood. A false inclusion on an identity series is worse than a false exclusion.
Exclusion, restrictive covenants and redlining are stated plainly, in those words; a story never closes on the injury alone.
Keep titles and distinctions (Reverend, Doctor; the first, the only).
series._historyLineYears: The author, 2026-10-05: a life is history once the part of it a story tells is at least this many years past, as landmark practice asks of a place. A sitting officeholder is not history yet; a mayor of the 1990s may be. tools/survey.py draws the line on the long list; the scout applies it (PLAYBOOK §1).

survey._comment: The long list (tools/survey.py, 2026-10-05): leads from the encyclopedias that cover this community person by person, never members. Identity still comes from a dossier and the identity check.

sources.label: BlackPast, entries whose text names the place
Wikipedia, the fame.py run's identity screen

book._comment: The series as one book (tools/series_book.py, 2026-10-05): a companion to the landmark guide, in the order the subjects arrived. A story files itself into the part its arrival year falls in; a part with no story yet is not shown.
book.title: Black Seattle
book.subtitle: Lives from the record, from the settler town to the civil-rights years
book.intro: Black Seattleites in the order they arrived, from the town's first decade on. Each story is told from the public record and cites it paragraph by paragraph, and the places they lived, worked and worshipped link to the Seattle Landmarks guide.

parts.title: The war and the civil-rights years

series.title: Indigenous Seattle
series._titleNote: Not 'Native Seattle': that is the title of Coll Thrush's 2007 history.
series.membership: Coast Salish people of the place now called Seattle, and the Alaska Native and other Indigenous people the city's record holds.
scoutHints: leaders and families named in treaty-era and later records
people who kept homes on the shoreline and in the city after removal
Indigenous workers, artists and activists of the twentieth century
sources authored or co-authored by the Duwamish, Suquamish and Muckleshoot nations
sensitivity: Use each nation's own names for itself and its people.
No ceremonial or sacred detail, even when a source prints it.
Federal recognition status is stated as a dated fact and never argued.
Prefer sources the nations authored; settler sources are read against the grain for facts, never for framing.

series.title: Settler Seattle
series.membership: People who came to build the settler town and city, chosen by the record they left rather than by fame.
scoutHints: prefer the people the standard accounts skip: tradespeople, boarding-house keepers, clerks, small merchants, immigrants of the 1880s–1910s
a famous founder only when the record holds something the hundred earlier histories missed
sensitivity: The settler town was built on Duwamish land; say so plainly where it touches the story, without a sermon.
Use 'settler', never 'pioneer' as a term of praise.
